turns.prompt_text: What is ssh -L
turns.response_html:
The -L flag in SSH stands for Local Port Forwarding. It allows you to take a port on your local machine and "tunnel" it through an SSH connection to a specific port on a remote server.

Think of it as creating a secure pipe. You plug one end into your laptop and the other end into a service running on a remote network that you normally couldn't reach directly.

How the Syntax Works

The standard structure for the command is:

ssh -L [local_ip:]local_port:destination_host:destination_port user@ssh_server

ComponentDescription
local_portThe port on your machine you want to use (e.g., 8080).
destination_hostThe address of the server you want to reach from the perspective of the SSH server.
destination_portThe port the service is actually running on (e.g., 3306 for MySQL).
user@ssh_serverThe middleman—the server you are actually SSHing into.

Common Use Cases

1. Accessing a Remote Web Interface

Imagine you have a Jupyter Notebook or a database dashboard running on a remote server at port 8888, but the server's firewall blocks external access to that port.

ssh -L 8000:localhost:8888 user@remote-server.com

Now, if you open your local browser and go to http://localhost:8000, you are actually seeing what is running on the remote server's port 8888.

2. Using a "Jump Box" to Reach a Private Database

Suppose you have a database on a private IP (10.0.0.50) that you can't reach from home, but you can SSH into a public web server that has access to that private network.

ssh -L 3333:10.0.0.50:3306 user@public-web-server.com

Your local machine now thinks the database is running at localhost:3333. Your database management tool (like MySQL Workbench) can connect to that local port, and the traffic will be securely tunneled through the web server to the private database.

Why use it?

  • Security: Your data is encrypted inside the SSH tunnel, even if the application protocol (like HTTP or VNC) isn't.
  • Bypassing Firewalls: It allows you to access services that aren't exposed to the public internet.
  • Convenience: You can use local tools to manage remote resources without complex VPN setups.

Are you trying to bypass a specific firewall restriction, or are you setting up a secure tunnel for a database?

turns.prompt_text: I have my mac air with me in Ames, and my Mac Mini is in Ankeny, I am connected via ssh, and I am attempting to screen share as well my Mac Mini to my Mac Air
turns.response_html:
To securely tunnel Screen Sharing (which uses the VNC protocol) from your Mac Mini to your MacBook Air, you will use the -L flag to forward the VNC port. By default, macOS Screen Sharing operates on port 5900.

It is often best to map the remote port to 5901 on your MacBook Air. This prevents any conflict if Screen Sharing is already running locally on your Air.

1. Establish the SSH Tunnel

Run this command from the terminal on your MacBook Air:

ssh -L 5901:localhost:5900 user@remote_address
  • 5901: The port on your MacBook Air you will connect to.
  • localhost:5900: Tells the Mac Mini to take traffic from the tunnel and send it to its own Screen Sharing service.
  • user@remote_address: Your login credentials for the Mac Mini in Ankeny.

Keep this terminal window open. If you close it or the SSH session times out, the "pipe" will break and the screen share will disconnect.

2. Launch the Connection

Once the SSH session is active, you can initiate the visual connection. You do not need to type in the remote IP address into the Screen Sharing app; you point it at the local end of your tunnel.

  1. Open the Screen Sharing app (or press Cmd + Space and type "Screen Sharing").
  2. In the "Connect To" or "Host" field, enter: localhost:5901
  3. Enter the username and password for the Mac Mini when prompted.

Alternatively, you can run this command in a second terminal tab to launch it instantly:

open vnc://localhost:5901

3. Verification & Requirements

For this to function, ensure the following settings are active on the Mac Mini:

  • Remote Login: Must be enabled under System Settings > General > Sharing (this allows the SSH connection).
  • Screen Sharing: Must be enabled under System Settings > General > Sharing.
  • Sleep Settings: Ensure the Mac Mini is not set to go to sleep, or that "Wake for network access" is enabled, otherwise the SSH connection will drop.

Pro-Tip: Compression

Since you are connecting between Ames and Ankeny over the internet, adding the -C flag can improve performance by compressing the data stream:

ssh -C -L 5901:localhost:5900 user@remote_address

Would you like the specific terminal commands to verify if the Screen Sharing service is currently active on the remote machine?

turns.prompt_text: Does this work over ipv6? And must I already be sshed in before I ssh -L
turns.response_html:
Yes, it absolutely works over IPv6, and you do not need a pre-existing connection to set it up. In fact, ssh -L is the command that initiates the connection itself.

1. Using IPv6 for the Tunnel

SSH supports IPv6 natively. If your network in Ames and the network in Ankeny both have IPv6 connectivity, you can force SSH to use it by adding the -6 flag.

The Command:

ssh -6 -L 5901:[::1]:5900 user@your-ipv6-address
  • -6: Forces SSH to use IPv6 addresses.
  • [::1]: This is the IPv6 equivalent of localhost. When the tunnel reaches your Mac Mini, it tells the Mini to look at its own internal IPv6 loopback for the Screen Sharing service.
  • The Address: Ensure the remote address you use at the end is either the Mac Mini’s global IPv6 address or a hostname that resolves to one.

2. Connection Order: Do you need to be SSH'd in first?

No. The -L flag is an argument you pass to the initial ssh command. It builds the tunnel at the same time it opens your terminal session.

  • Scenario A (Standard): You run ssh -L ... from a fresh terminal. It asks for your password, logs you in, and the tunnel is "live" for as long as that window stays open.
  • Scenario B (If you are already logged in): If you already have a standard SSH window open without the tunnel, you have two choices:
    1. Exit and Re-run: Close the current session and run the command again with the -L flag added.
    2. The "Escape" Method: You can actually add a tunnel to an active session without disconnecting.
      • In your active SSH window, press Enter.
      • Type ~C (Shift + Tilde, then Capital C).
      • The prompt will change to ssh>.
      • Type -L 5901:localhost:5900 and press Enter.
      • The tunnel is now active in your existing session.

Key Requirements for IPv6

Since you are connecting between two different cities, IPv6 can sometimes be more reliable for "reaching through" routers without complex port forwarding, provided:

  1. Global Unicast Addresses: Both Macs have a public-facing IPv6 address (usually starting with 2001:).
  2. Firewall: The Mac Mini’s local firewall (and the Ankeny router's firewall) must specifically allow incoming traffic on Port 22 for IPv6.

Are you using a Global IPv6 address to connect, or are you relying on a local hostname like macmini.local?

turns.prompt_text: How can I enable screen sharing via command line in the Mac Mini? I have super user privileges
turns.response_html:
Since you are already logged in via SSH with superuser privileges, the most reliable way to toggle Screen Sharing is through the kickstart utility. This is a built-in macOS tool designed specifically for managing Remote Management and Screen Sharing services from the command line.

The "Hammer" Method (Apple Remote Desktop)

This command enables the full suite of remote management features. It is the most effective way to ensure the service is live and permissions are granted to all users.

Run this single command on the Mac Mini:

sudo /System/Library/CoreServices/RemoteManagement/ARDHelper.app/Contents/Resources/kickstart -activate -configure -access -on -restart -agent -privs -all

What this does:

  • -activate: Turns the service on.
  • -configure -access -on: Enables access.
  • -restart -agent: Restarts the background process to ensure it picks up the changes.
  • -privs -all: Grants the connecting user full permissions (virtual mouse control, file transfer, etc.).

The "Scalpel" Method (Screen Sharing Only)

If you prefer to enable only the basic Screen Sharing service without the extra Apple Remote Desktop overhead, you can use launchctl. This is more "surgical" but sometimes requires a secondary command to bypass the system firewall.

  1. Enable the service:

    sudo launchctl load -w /System/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.apple.screensharing.plist

  2. Verify it is running:

    sudo launchctl list | grep screensharing

    If you see a PID (a number in the first column), the service is active.

Troubleshooting Common Blocks

Even with the service "on," macOS security layers (TCC) can sometimes block the connection if it wasn't previously configured in the UI.

1. Check the Firewall

If the Mac Mini has the macOS Firewall turned on, it might be blocking port 5900 even if the service is running. You can globally allow Screen Sharing through the firewall with:

sudo /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterproxy --add /System/Library/CoreServices/RemoteManagement/ScreensharingAgent.bundle/Contents/MacOS/ScreensharingAgent

2. Verify Port Listening

To make sure the Mac Mini is actually listening for your SSH tunnel on port 5900, run:

netstat -an | grep 5900

You should see a line ending in *.5900 LISTEN.

[!IMPORTANT] Privacy Note: On newer versions of macOS (Sonoma/Sequoia), even if you enable Screen Sharing via CLI, the OS may trigger a "Screen Recording" permission prompt on the remote screen. Since you aren't physically in Ankeny to click "Allow," the kickstart method remains your best bet as it generally bypasses these user-level prompts when run with sudo.

Are you seeing any "Connection Refused" errors when you try to launch the VNC app on your MacBook Air, or is the terminal tunnel establishing correctly?

turns.prompt_text: `sudo: /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterproxy: command not found` There is a socketfilterfw or a socketfilterhelper
turns.response_html:
You're right to catch that—Apple shifted the naming and paths in recent macOS versions. socketfilterfw is the correct binary for managing the Application Firewall from the terminal now.

Here is how to use socketfilterfw to ensure your Screen Sharing traffic isn't being dropped.

1. Check Firewall Status

First, see if the firewall is even active. If it's off, the issue lies elsewhere (likely the SSH tunnel or the service itself).

sudo /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --getglobalstate

2. Allow Screen Sharing (The Agent)

If the firewall is on, you need to explicitly tell it to allow the ScreensharingAgent. This is the background process that handles the actual VNC data.

Add the application to the exception list:

sudo /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --add /System/Library/CoreServices/RemoteManagement/ScreensharingAgent.bundle/Contents/MacOS/ScreensharingAgent

Set it to allow incoming connections:

sudo /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --unblockapp /System/Library/CoreServices/RemoteManagement/ScreensharingAgent.bundle/Contents/MacOS/ScreensharingAgent

3. Enable "Built-in" Software Exceptions

macOS has a toggle to automatically allow signed software (like Apple's own Screen Sharing) to receive connections. Turning this on can often fix connection issues without manual path entries:

sudo /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --setallowsigned on

4. Restart the Firewall Service

For the changes to take effect immediately, kick the process so it reloads its configuration:

sudo pkill -HUP socketfilterfw

Is the service actually listening?

Since you are in Ames trying to hit a machine in Ankeny, you want to be 100% sure the Mini is ready for your tunnel. Run this on the Mini:

sudo lsof -i -P | grep -i listen | grep 5900
  • If you see nothing: Screen Sharing isn't actually running yet. Try the kickstart command from the previous message again.
  • If you see Screenshar (LISTEN): The service is up and the firewall is the only thing that could be blocking it locally.

One IPv6 Specific Note

If you are using a Global IPv6 address, sometimes the router in Ankeny has its own IPv6 firewall that blocks all incoming traffic by default, regardless of what the Mac Mini says. If the tunnel itself connects (the SSH part), then your router is fine. If the SSH connection itself times out, you may need to check the Ankeny router settings to allow Port 22 over IPv6.

Does the SSH connection establish, or are you getting a "Connection Refused/Timed Out" before you even get to the Screen Sharing step?

turns.prompt_text: `Make sure Screen Sharing or Remote Management (in the Sharing section of System Settings) is enabled on the remote computer.`
turns.response_html:
That error message is the classic "handshake" failure. It means your MacBook Air successfully talked to the local end of your tunnel, but when the tunnel tried to pass that data to port 5900 on your Mac Mini, nobody was home—or the door was locked.

Since you've already tried the standard kickstart command, let's use a more aggressive method to force the service to wake up and verify exactly where the break is.

Step 1: Verify the "Listener" on the Mac Mini

Run this on the Mac Mini via your existing SSH session to see if the Screen Sharing service is actually awake and waiting:

sudo lsof -i :5900
  • If the output is empty: The service is not running.
  • If you see Screenshar (LISTEN): The service is running, but the tunnel might be pointing to the wrong "localhost" (IPv4 vs. IPv6).

Step 2: The "Force Start" (For Modern macOS)

If lsof showed nothing, the kickstart command might have been blocked by modern macOS security. Try this specific sequence to override the disable flag and force-load the daemon:

# 1. Remove the "Disabled" flag from the launch database
sudo defaults write /var/db/launchd.db/com.apple.launchd/overrides.plist com.apple.screensharing -dict Disabled -bool false

# 2. Force load the service
sudo launchctl load -w /System/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.apple.screensharing.plist

After running these, run sudo lsof -i :5900 again. If it now says LISTEN, try connecting from your Air.

Step 3: Check the "Loopback" Ambiguity

If you are using IPv6 for the SSH connection, the tunnel might be trying to connect to the IPv6 loopback ([::1]) while the Screen Sharing service is only listening on the IPv4 loopback (127.0.0.1).

Try establishing your tunnel using the explicit IPv4 loopback for the destination. On your MacBook Air, close your current SSH session and run:

ssh -L 5901:127.0.0.1:5900 user@remote_address

(By using 127.0.0.1 instead of localhost, you bypass any confusion about which "local" the computer should use.)

Step 4: The "Privacy" Permission Bypass

If the service is listening but you still get the error, it's possible the Mac Mini is asking for "Screen Recording" permission on a screen you can't see.

You can try to grant permissions to the Screen Sharing agent directly via the TCC database (this is the "nuclear option" for CLI users):

sudo sqlite3 /Library/Application\ Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db "INSERT OR REPLACE INTO access VALUES('kTCCServiceScreenCapture','com.apple.screensharing.agent',0,2,4,1,NULL,NULL,0,'UNUSED',NULL,0,$(date +%s));"

Summary Checklist

  1. On Mini: Run sudo lsof -i :5900. Is it listening?
  2. On Air: Run lsof -i :5901. Is your SSH tunnel actually holding that port open?
  3. On Air: Try connecting to vnc://127.0.0.1:5901 instead of localhost:5901.

If you run sudo lsof -i :5900 on the Mini and it still returns nothing after the launchctl command, let me know—that implies a deeper system policy is blocking the service from starting.

turns.prompt_text: current state: mac air in ames, mac mini in Ankeny, mac air is sshed into mac mini with vnc and in another pane with plain ssh, both through ipv6 lsof on the mini shows it is listening: ``` sudo lsof -i :5900 Password: COMMAND PID USER FD TYPE DEVICE SIZE/OFF NODE NAME launchd 1 root 19u IPv6 0x813536954946714 0t0 TCP *:rfb (LISTEN) launchd 1 root 20u IPv4 0xc58cdd767c101298 0t0 TCP *:rfb (LISTEN) launchd 1 root 24u IPv6 0x813536954946714 0t0 TCP *:rfb (LISTEN) launchd 1 root 56u IPv4 0xc58cdd767c101298 0t0 TCP *:rfb (LISTEN) ``` lsof on the mac air ``` lsof -i :5901 COMMAND PID USER FD TYPE DEVICE SIZE/OFF NODE NAME Screen 76132 arognes 3u IPv6 0xf5ee619bf8e5cea6 0t0 TCP localhost:59928->localhost:5901 (CLOSED) ```
turns.response_html:
The fact that lsof -i :5901 on your MacBook Air shows a CLOSED state and—more importantly—doesn't show the ssh process is the "smoking gun."

Usually, if the tunnel is active, you should see an entry for ssh (or ssh-backend) with a status of LISTEN on port 5901. Right now, your Screen Sharing app is knocking on the door of port 5901, but since SSH isn't actually holding that door open, the connection is immediately rejected.

Here is how to get that tunnel locked in.

1. The "Double-Stack" Tunnel Command

Since you are using IPv6 to bridge the gap between Ames and Ankeny, let's use a command that explicitly binds to the IPv4 loopback on the remote side. This bypasses a common macOS bug where launchd listens on IPv6 but expects traffic from the tunnel to arrive via IPv4.

Run this on your MacBook Air (close your existing VNC tunnel pane first):

ssh -6 -L 5901:127.0.0.1:5900 user@your-ankeny-ipv6-address

Why this works:

  • -6: Forces the "long-distance" connection to stay on IPv6.
  • 127.0.0.1:5900: Once the traffic reaches the Mini, it forces the data to be handed off to the internal IPv4 loopback, which is usually more reliable for the rfb (Screen Sharing) service.

2. Verify the Tunnel on the Air

Before you even touch the Screen Sharing app, run this on the MacBook Air:

lsof -nP -iTCP:5901 -sTCP:LISTEN
  • If you see nothing: The SSH tunnel failed to bind to the port. Check the terminal for "Address already in use" or "Permission denied."
  • If you see ssh or sshd and LISTEN: Your pipe is officially open.

3. Connect via explicit IP

Sometimes the macOS "Screen Sharing" app gets confused by the word localhost because it might try to resolve it to ::1 (IPv6) while the tunnel is listening on 127.0.0.1 (IPv4).

In the Screen Sharing app "Connect to" box, type exactly this: 127.0.0.1:5901

(Avoid using the word localhost for this specific test.)

4. Troubleshooting the "Silent Killer" (Sleep)

If the lsof on the Mini showed launchd listening but the connection still won't "catch," it might be because the Mini has transitioned into a "Dark Wake" state or the display is asleep.

Since you have an active SSH session on the Mini, wake it up with this command:

sudo caffeinate -u -t 60

This simulates a user interaction to ensure the Screen Sharing service is fully prioritized by the kernel.

A quick check for you:

When you ran the ssh -L command on your Air, did the terminal give you any specific error message right after you entered your password? (e.g., “channel_setup_fwd_listener-listen: port 5901: error binding”)

turns.prompt_text: Current state: Mac air sshed into Mac Mini via `ssh -6 -L 5901:127.0.0.1:5900 austinrognes@fd7a:115c:a1e0:9a33:4161` and is running smoothly Mac air ran ` lsof -nP -iTCP:5901 -sTCP:LISTEN` with a blank line of output
turns.response_html:
If you are successfully logged into the Mac Mini via SSH, but lsof on your MacBook Air shows nothing listening on port 5901, then the tunnel failed to "bind" locally even though the terminal session itself succeeded.

SSH often fails "silently" regarding tunnels—it will let you log in to the shell but skip the port forwarding if it encounters an error.

1. The "Verbose" Debugging Step

To see exactly why the tunnel isn't being created, run the command again with the -v (verbose) flag. This will output the handshake details.

On your MacBook Air, close the current session and run:

ssh -v -6 -L 5901:127.0.0.1:5900 austinrognes@fd7a:115c:a1e0:9a33:4161

Look for these specific lines in the wall of text:

  • debug1: Local connections to 127.0.0.1:5901 forwarded to remote 127.0.0.1:5900
  • debug1: Local forwarding listening on 127.0.0.1 port 5901.
  • OR an error like: channel_setup_fwd_listener-listen: port 5901: Address already in use or Permission denied.

2. Try an Alternative Port

If port 5901 is stuck in a "TIME_WAIT" state from your previous attempts, the OS might prevent SSH from grabbing it again immediately. Try a "high" port that is unlikely to be used:

ssh -6 -L 8888:127.0.0.1:5900 austinrognes@fd7a:115c:a1e0:9a33:4161

Then, check lsof -i :8888 on the Air. If that shows a LISTEN state for the ssh process, you can connect your Screen Sharing app to 127.0.0.1:8888.

3. Check the Mac Mini’s SSH Configuration

It is possible that the Mac Mini's SSH server is configured to allow login but disallow port forwarding.

On the Mac Mini (in your active SSH pane), check the configuration file:

grep "AllowTcpForwarding" /etc/ssh/sshd_config
  • If it says AllowTcpForwarding no: This is your culprit.
  • To fix it:
    1. sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config
    2. Change it to AllowTcpForwarding yes (or just comment the line out, as yes is the default).
    3. Restart the SSH service: 
      sudo launchctl unload /System/Library/LaunchDaemons/ssh.plist
sudo launchctl load -w /System/Library/LaunchDaemons/ssh.plist

4. Binding to IPv6 Localhost

Since you are connecting over IPv6, your MacBook Air might be trying to bind the local end of the tunnel to the IPv6 loopback (::1) while you are checking the IPv4 loopback (127.0.0.1).

Try forcing the bind to IPv4 on the local side:

ssh -L 127.0.0.1:5901:127.0.0.1:5900 -6 austinrognes@[fd7a:115c:a1e0:9a33:4161]

(Note: Adding brackets around the IPv6 address is standard syntax when using more complex flags to prevent the colons from being misinterpreted.)

Verification Checklist

  • On the Air: Does lsof -nP -i :5901 now show ssh as the COMMAND and LISTEN as the STATE?
  • On the Air: If you run telnet 127.0.0.1 5901, does it say "Connected" or "Connection refused"?

When you run the verbose (-v) command, do you see any "Local forwarding listening" messages, or does it mention a "Forwarding error"?

turns.prompt_text: running on mac mini:`grep "AllowTcpForwarding" /etc/ssh/sshd_config` returned ``` #AllowTcpForwarding yes # AllowTcpForwarding no ``` I found a typo in the ssh -v -6 -L command. Running `open vnc://[::1]:590` now opens the "Connecting to '::1':5901" But then I get ``` Unable to communicate with “[::1]:5901”. Make sure the remote computer is available and the firewall is not blocking screen sharing. ```
turns.response_html:
This is the final hurdle: the loopback mismatch.

When you run ssh -L 5901:127.0.0.1:5900, SSH by default binds the local port (5901) to your IPv4 loopback (127.0.0.1). However, when you run open vnc://[::1]:5901, you are telling the Screen Sharing app to look for the tunnel on your IPv6 loopback ([::1]).

Even though they both mean "this machine," they are different logical interfaces. If SSH is listening on one, and the VNC app is looking at the other, they won't see each other.

1. The Quickest Fix

Try connecting to the IPv4 loopback address in the Screen Sharing app. This is the most likely way to "catch" the tunnel you just built.

Run this on your MacBook Air:

open vnc://127.0.0.1:5901

2. The "Universal" Tunnel Command

If you prefer to use the IPv6 loopback ([::1]), you have to explicitly tell SSH to bind the local end of the tunnel to it.

On your MacBook Air, try this command:

ssh -6 -L [::1]:5901:127.0.0.1:5900 austinrognes@fd7a:115c:a1e0:9a33:4161
  • [::1]:5901: Binds the local end to IPv6 loopback.
  • 127.0.0.1:5900: Hands off to the Mini's internal IPv4 loopback (where we know it's listening).

Then you can use:

open vnc://[::1]:5901

3. Verify the Local Bind

To be absolutely certain where your MacBook Air is "hosting" the tunnel, run this on the Air while the SSH session is active:

lsof -nP -i :5901 | grep LISTEN

Look at the "NAME" column:

  • If it says 127.0.0.1:5901, use vnc://127.0.0.1:5901.
  • If it says [::1]:5901, use vnc://[::1]:5901.
  • If it says *:5901, you can use either!

4. A Note on macOS "High-Performance" Screen Sharing

Since you are likely on a recent macOS version (given the Mac Mini/Air setup), the "Screen Sharing" app sometimes tries to be too smart and might be trying to use its own high-performance protocol (which uses different ports).

If you get a password prompt but then the "Unable to communicate" error, it’s a permission/firewall issue. If you get "Unable to communicate" immediately without a password prompt, the VNC app isn't even seeing the tunnel.

One last check: In your ssh -v output, did you see a line that says debug1: Entering interactive session.? That confirms the tunnel is technically "open" and just waiting for traffic.

Does lsof on the Air finally show the ssh process in a LISTEN state now?

turns.prompt_text: `open vnc://127.0.0.1:5901`: ``` Make sure Screen Sharing or Remote Management (in the Sharing section of System Settings) is enabled on the remote computer. ```
turns.response_html:
This specific error, while the tunnel is active and the service is listening, almost always points to a permissions or authentication block on the Mac Mini. Even if the "door" is open, the Mac Mini is refusing to let the connection in because it doesn't recognize the request as authorized.

Since you have that verbose (-v) SSH window open, look at it the moment you try to connect via VNC. If you see a message like channel 3: open failed: connect failed: Connection refused, the tunnel is working but the Mac Mini's VNC server is hanging up on it.

1. Explicitly Grant Your User Permissions

Sometimes the kickstart command enables the service but doesn't correctly "link" your user account to the allowed list in the system's security database.

Run this on the Mac Mini:

sudo /System/Library/CoreServices/RemoteManagement/ARDHelper.app/Contents/Resources/kickstart -configure -access -on -privs -all -users austinrognes

2. Bypass the "Localhost" VNC Block

macOS Screen Sharing sometimes has a security policy that ignores VNC requests coming from 127.0.0.1 (the tunnel) because it thinks it’s a security loop. You can try to tell the Screen Sharing agent to allow all connections, even "local" ones.

Run this on the Mac Mini:

sudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/com.apple.RemoteManagement.plist VNCPrivilegeSoftwareGuestMode -bool TRUE
sudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/com.apple.RemoteManagement.plist AlwaysAllowVNC -bool TRUE

3. Kick the Screensharing Agent

If the service is "Listening" but unresponsive, the background agent might be hung. Force it to restart:

sudo killall ScreensharingAgent

(Don't worry, launchd will immediately restart it because you enabled it earlier.)

4. Try the "Legacy" VNC Password

If the macOS "Screen Sharing" app is failing, it might be due to the modern encrypted authentication handshake failing over a tunnel. Setting a classic VNC password can sometimes bridge this.

Run this on the Mac Mini:

sudo /System/Library/CoreServices/RemoteManagement/ARDHelper.app/Contents/Resources/kickstart -configure -clientopts -setvncpasswd -vncpasswd yourpassword

Then, try connecting from your Air again.

The "Diagnostic" Check

If none of that works, we need to see if the Mac Mini allows any connection to port 5900 from itself. Run this on the Mac Mini:

nc -zv 127.0.0.1 5900
  • If it says "Succeeded!": The port is 100% open and the issue is purely a macOS software permission/UI block.
  • If it says "Connection refused": The service is "listening" (as seen in lsof) but the kernel is dropping the packets. This usually means the macOS Firewall is still the culprit.

When you try to connect, does the SSH verbose (-v) window on your Air show any new text appearing? If it says open failed, the problem is on the Mini. If it says nothing at all, the VNC app isn't even hitting the tunnel.

turns.prompt_text: This is the output from the previously run ssh -v -6 -L command, no new commands have been run: ``` Send job 1 (ssh -v -6 -L 5901:127.0.0.1:5900 austinrognes@fd7a:115c:a1e0::9a33:4161 &) to foreground tcsetattr: Interrupted system call debug1: Connection to port 5901 forwarding to 127.0.0.1 port 590 ```
turns.response_html:
That debug line is the "Aha!" moment. Looking closely at the end of your log:

debug1: Connection to port 5901 forwarding to 127.0.0.1 port 590

You are missing a zero! You have successfully built a tunnel to Port 590, but macOS Screen Sharing lives on Port 5900. Because nothing is listening on 590 on the Mac Mini, the connection is being dropped immediately.

The Fix

Close your current SSH session and run the command with the corrected remote port:

ssh -6 -L 5901:127.0.0.1:5900 austinrognes@fd7a:115c:a1e0:9a33:4161

Once you are logged in, try the connection from your MacBook Air again:

open vnc://127.0.0.1:5901

Why this happened

When you specify -L 5901:127.0.0.1:590, SSH dutifully creates a listener on your Air (5901), but it tries to "talk" to port 590 on the Mini.

  • Port 5900: Standard VNC/Screen Sharing.
  • Port 590: Usually used for the "Free-format Directory Service" (old and unrelated).

A Note on the "Interrupted system call"

The tcsetattr: Interrupted system call message in your log usually happens when you move an SSH process from the background (&) to the foreground (fg). It’s a minor terminal quirk and shouldn't affect the tunnel once the command is running properly.

How to verify it's working now

In your ssh -v window, after you run the open vnc command, you should now see a new line appear that looks like this: debug1: Connection to port 5901 forwarding to 127.0.0.1 port 5900 requested.

If you see the 5900 at the end of that request, you should finally see the login window for your Mac Mini.

Give that corrected command a shot—does it prompt you for a password on the Mac Mini now?

turns.response_html:
The log tells a very specific story: the tunnel is being created, but as soon as the Screen Sharing app tries to use it, the connection is being dropped with an Invalid argument error.

The getpeername failed: Invalid argument error on macOS often happens when there is a mismatch between how the application (Screen Sharing) is trying to talk to the local port and how SSH is listening to it. Specifically, your log shows a "cross-talk" attempt: connect from 127.0.0.1... to ::1 port 5901. Your app is trying to use IPv6 locally while the tunnel might be expecting IPv4.

Here is the "Golden Path" to fix this:

1. Don't Background the Command Yet

The tcsetattr and tty errors in your log suggest that running the command with & is causing some terminal interference. Let's run it in the foreground so we can see the errors in real-time.

2. The "Bind-All" Command

We are going to force SSH to listen on both the IPv4 and IPv6 loopback interfaces on your MacBook Air. This prevents the Screen Sharing app from getting confused.

Run this on your MacBook Air:

ssh -v -6 -L 127.0.0.1:5901:127.0.0.1:5900 -L [::1]:5901:127.0.0.1:5900 austinrognes@fd7a:115c:a1e0::9a33:4161

Why this version?

  • Double -L: It opens the tunnel on both 127.0.0.1 (IPv4) and [::1] (IPv6) locally. No matter which one the macOS Screen Sharing app picks, the tunnel will be there.
  • No &: It stays in the foreground so it doesn't get "Killed by signal 2" or interrupted by system calls.

3. Launch the Connection

Once that terminal says Entering interactive session, go to your browser or the Screen Sharing app and use this exact address:

vnc://127.0.0.1:5901

(Using the IP address instead of localhost or ::1 forces macOS to stay on the IPv4 path, which is much more stable for SSH tunneling.)

4. Troubleshooting the Invalid argument Error

If you still see setsockopt TCP_NODELAY: Invalid argument, this is sometimes a quirk of connecting over certain network types (like a mesh VPN or specific IPv6 tunnels). You can tell SSH to stop trying to optimize the socket delay, which often bypasses this error.

Add -o "IPQoS=throughput" to your command:

ssh -6 -o "IPQoS=throughput" -L 5901:127.0.0.1:5900 austinrognes@fd7a:115c:a1e0::9a33:4161

5. Check for "Ghost" Tunnels

Your log showed Killed by signal 2, but sometimes the process doesn't actually die and it keeps holding onto the port. If you get an "Address already in use" error, run this to kill any lingering SSH tunnels:

ps aux | grep ssh | grep 5901 | awk '{print $2}' | xargs kill -9

Summary of what to look for in the log:

When you hit "Connect" in the Screen Sharing app, look for this line in your verbose SSH terminal: debug1: channel 2: connected to 127.0.0.1 port 5900

If you see connected instead of free, you're in.

Does the 127.0.0.1:5901 address get you past the "Unable to communicate" error now that the tunnel is explicitly bound?

turns.prompt_text: running the ssh double -L flag, then the vnc command gives this popup window: ``` Make sure Screen Sharing or Remote Management (in the Sharing section of System Settings) is enabled on the remote computer. ```
turns.response_html:
This error indicates that while the "port" is open, the Mac Mini is actively rejecting the connection attempt. Since lsof showed launchd is listening on port 5900, the "socket" is there, but the actual ScreensharingAgent is likely failing to hand off the connection.

Here is the sequence to force the service into a clean state and bypass the most common macOS security blocks.

1. Test the "Local" Handshake

On the Mac Mini (via your SSH pane), run this to see if the machine can talk to itself on that port. This determines if the issue is the tunnel or the service:

nc -zv 127.0.0.1 5900
  • If it says Connection refused: The service is dead or the firewall is hard-blocking it.
  • If it says Succeeded!: The service is alive, but it is rejecting your MacBook Air specifically due to a permission or authentication mismatch.

2. Resolve the "Sharing" Conflict

macOS cannot run "Screen Sharing" and "Remote Management" (ARD) at the same time. If both are partially enabled, they will fight for port 5900 and fail. Run this to full-reset the service:

# Deactivate both services entirely
sudo /System/Library/CoreServices/RemoteManagement/ARDHelper.app/Contents/Resources/kickstart -deactivate -stop

# Re-activate only Screen Sharing with full permissions
sudo /System/Library/CoreServices/RemoteManagement/ARDHelper.app/Contents/Resources/kickstart -activate -configure -access -on -restart -agent -privs -all

3. The "Headless" Mac Mini Issue

If your Mac Mini in Ankeny does not have a monitor plugged into it, the macOS window server may refuse to start a graphical session. This is a common "feature" of Mac Minis.

To force the Mac to "wake up" the virtual display for your session, run this in the SSH pane:

sudo caffeinate -u -t 60 &

If this still fails, you may eventually need a "Dummy HDMI plug" (Ghost Plug) for that Mini so it thinks a monitor is attached.

4. Bypassing the Authentication Handshake

Sometimes the encrypted Apple ID login fails over a tunnel. Enabling a "Legacy" VNC password often acts as a bypass.

  1. Set a VNC Password on the Mini: 
    sudo /System/Library/CoreServices/RemoteManagement/ARDHelper.app/Contents/Resources/kickstart -configure -clientopts -setvncpasswd -vncpasswd MyTemporaryPassword
  2. Try to connect from the Air again: When the Screen Sharing app opens, it may ask for a password. Use the one you just set.

5. Final Diagnostic: Check the Agent Logs

If you still get the error, check the Mini's system logs in real-time while you try to connect. Run this on the Mini:

log stream --predicate 'process == "ScreensharingAgent"'

Then, try to connect from the Air. Watch for messages like Authentication failed or Permission denied.

Summary Checklist for your next attempt:

  1. Ensure the tunnel is active (the double -L command).
  2. Use vnc://127.0.0.1:5901 in the Screen Sharing app.
  3. If it fails, look at the log stream output on the Mini.

Is your Mac Mini currently connected to a physical monitor, or is it running headless in Ankeny?

turns.prompt_text: Is there an easier way to go about this?
turns.response_html:
SSH tunneling for Screen Sharing can often feel like a game of technical whack-a-mole, especially when dealing with macOS's evolving security layers and IPv6/IPv4 loopback quirks.

If the manual "pipe" keeps leaking, there are three significantly easier ways to bridge the gap between Ames and Ankeny that bypass SSH configuration entirely.

1. Tailscale (The Modern "Gold Standard")

Tailscale creates a secure, private "Mesh VPN" using the WireGuard protocol. Instead of manual tunnels, it assigns each of your devices a stable, private IP address (like 100.x.y.z) that works anywhere in the world.

  • Why it’s easier: You don't need to manage ports, SSH flags, or IPv6 addresses.
  • The Setup: 1. Install Tailscale on the Mac Mini and the MacBook Air. 2. Log in with the same account. 3. On your MacBook Air, simply open the Screen Sharing app and type in the Tailscale IP of the Mac Mini.
  • Result: It "just works" as if the two Macs were sitting on the same desk.

2. Apple's Native "High Performance" Screen Sharing

If both Macs are running macOS Sonoma or later and are signed into the same Apple ID, you can use the built-in High Performance mode. This protocol is designed to work over the internet without a VPN or SSH tunnel.

  • Why it’s easier: It uses Apple’s own infrastructure to "find" your Mac Mini.
  • The Setup:
    1. On the Mac Mini, ensure Screen Sharing is enabled in System Settings > General > Sharing.
    2. On the MacBook Air, open the Screen Sharing app.
    3. Click the "+" sign and enter your Apple ID (email).
  • Result: It will list your Mac Mini as an available device. This mode also supports better frame rates and lower latency than standard VNC.

3. Jump Desktop (The "Pro" Utility)

Jump Desktop is a popular third-party app among power users. It uses a proprietary protocol called "Fluid" and handles all the networking automatically.

  • Why it’s easier: It handles "hole punching" (getting through routers) and headless Mac issues (where the screen stays black because no monitor is attached) much better than macOS's native tools.
  • The Setup: Install the "Jump Desktop Connect" app on the Mini and the "Jump Desktop" app on your Air.
  • Result: You get a one-click connection to your remote desktop with almost zero latency.

Comparison Table

MethodSetup EffortPerformanceCost
SSH TunnelingHigh (Manual)ModerateFree
TailscaleVery LowHighFree (Personal)
Apple ID / NativeLowestHighFree
Jump DesktopLowBestPaid App

A Quick Fix for "Headless" Issues

Since your Mac Mini is in Ankeny, if there is no monitor plugged into it, the Screen Sharing service might be failing simply because the Mac isn't "rendering" a desktop.

If you decide to stick with the SSH method, try running this on the Mini to see if it forces a window server response: sudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/com.apple.windowserver.plist DisplayResolutionEnabled -bool YES

Would you prefer to try setting up a mesh VPN like Tailscale, or should we do one last "deep dive" into the Mac Mini’s system logs to see exactly why it's rejecting the SSH handshake?

turns.response_html:
That is excellent news! It’s a great feeling when the tunnel finally "clicks" and the remote desktop pops up. That port 590 vs 5900 typo was a subtle one, but those extra zeros make all the difference in the world.

Now that you’re connected, here are two quick tips to keep that session stable and snappy:

  • Keep-Alive: Since you are going between cities, your ISP might drop "idle" connections. If you find the screen freezing after a few minutes of inactivity, you can add -o ServerAliveInterval=60 to your SSH command next time to keep the pipe open.
  • Compression: If the lag gets noticeable while dragging windows, remember that -C flag in your SSH command. It compresses the VNC data stream on the fly, which usually makes things feel much more responsive over long-distance connections.

turns.prompt_text: Can I run a command from my fish terminal to open the Tailsail screenshare?
turns.response_html:
Since you are using the Fish shell, you can create a simple function or abbreviation to launch that connection instantly without typing the IP every time.

Assuming you have Tailscale installed and running on both machines, here is the best way to handle it.

1. The One-Liner

If you know the Tailscale IP or the "MagicDNS" name (e.g., mac-mini.tailscale.net) of your Ankeny machine, run this from your terminal in Ames:

open vnc://[Tailscale-IP-or-Hostname]

2. A Persistent Fish Function

Since you optimize your workflow with Fish, you should add this to your configuration so you can just type a short command like remote-mac.

  1. Run funced remote-mac in your terminal.
  2. Paste the following into the editor:
function remote-mac
    # Replace 'mac-mini' with your actual Tailscale hostname or IP
    open vnc://mac-mini.tailscale.net
end
  1. Run funcsave remote-mac to save it to ~/.config/fish/functions/.

Now, whenever you want to jump in, just type remote-mac.

3. How to Find the Correct "Tailscale" Address

If you aren't sure what the address is, you can pull it directly from the Tailscale CLI on either machine:

  • On the Mac Mini (via your current SSH): Run tailscale ip -4 to get the internal Tailscale IP.
  • On your MacBook Air: Run tailscale status to see a list of all your connected devices and their addresses.

Why this is better than the SSH Tunnel

  • No Manual Ports: You don't have to remember -L 5901:localhost:5900.
  • Native Resolution: Tailscale is often fast enough that macOS will automatically negotiate "High Performance" mode, giving you better retina resolution than the standard VNC tunnel.
  • Stable Pipe: If your Wi-Fi blips in Ames, Tailscale will automatically reconnect the background "wire" without you having to restart an SSH session.

[!TIP] If you find yourself using this frequently, you can also use a Fish abbreviation for even faster typing: abbr -a ss "open vnc://mac-mini.tailscale.net" Now, typing ss and hitting Space will expand to the full command.

Does the tailscale status command show your Mac Mini as "online" from your laptop right now?

turns.prompt_text: Yes, but I don't want to use the ipv4 for this, I have the ipv6, I just can't get it to work with vnc username:ipv6, whereas with the screen share app, username@ipv6 works just fine
turns.response_html:
The reason your command is likely failing is due to how URIs handle the multiple colons found in an IPv6 address. When you type an IPv6 address into a terminal-based URI, the system gets confused between the colons in the address and the colon used to denote a port number.

To fix this, you must wrap the IPv6 address in square brackets [].

The Correct CLI Syntax

In the terminal, the open command expects a standard URI format. Use an @ symbol to separate your username from the host, and wrap the address in brackets:

open vnc://austinrognes@[fd7a:115c:a1e0::9a33:4161]

Why the Brackets Matter

In networking standards (RFC 3986), the square brackets tell the parser, "Everything inside here is the IP address; stop looking for port colons until you reach the closing bracket." Without them, the Mac thinks you're trying to connect to a port named a1e0 or 9a33, which doesn't exist.

Automating it in Fish

Since you’re using the Fish shell and mentioned optimizing your workflow, you can bake this into a function. This saves you from ever having to remember the brackets or the long hex string again.

  1. Create the function: 
    function mini
    open vnc://austinrognes@[fd7a:115c:a1e0::9a33:4161]
end
  2. Save it permanently: 
    funcsave mini

Now, simply typing mini in your terminal will trigger the IPv6 screen share instantly.

Troubleshooting Tips

  • Username Mismatch: Ensure the username in the URI matches the short name of your account on the Mac Mini (usually lowercase, no spaces).
  • The @ vs :: While some apps are flexible, the standard URI protocol uses user@host. Using user:host often causes the shell to misinterpret the string as a variable or a malformed port.
  • Tailscale IPv6: If you are using the Tailscale IPv6 address specifically, ensure the Tailscale daemon is active on your MacBook Air. You can check this by running tailscale status.

Are you planning to set up any other terminal shortcuts for this remote environment, like a specific Neovim configuration sync?

turns.prompt_text: very nice, does vnc have a flag so I can use Standard screen sharing type and not high-performance?
turns.response_html:
While the open command doesn't have a specific command-line flag (like --standard) to toggle modes, macOS determines the connection type based on the URI scheme and your saved preferences for that specific host.

By default, using vnc:// in the terminal usually triggers the Standard (RFB-based) protocol. The "High Performance" mode is a newer Apple-specific feature (for Apple Silicon to Apple Silicon) that generally uses the vm-connect:// scheme or is toggled manually within the app.

If your Mac is being "too smart" and trying to upgrade you to High Performance automatically, here is how you can force it back to Standard from the terminal.

1. The "Standard" URI

In most cases, specifying the protocol as vnc:// (as you’ve done) is the "Standard" signal. High Performance is often initiated via a different internal handshake. If the Screen Sharing app opens and shows the "High Performance" badge in the toolbar, it has upgraded the connection.

2. Force Standard via defaults

You can tell the Screen Sharing app to default to Standard (VNC) globally or check your current setting using the defaults command. This is perfect for your Fish shell setup.

To set the default connection type to Standard, run this on your MacBook Air:

defaults write com.apple.ScreenSharing "lastSelectedConnectionType" -int 1
  • -int 1: Standard (VNC)
  • -int 2: High Performance

3. Comparison of Modes

Since you're optimizing for your remote setup, it's worth noting why you might pick one over the other:

FeatureStandard (VNC)High Performance
ProtocolRFB (Traditional)H.264 / H.265 (Hardware Encoded)
Color8-bit / 16-bit10-bit HDR / 4:4:4 Chroma
LatencyModerate (Good for Ames-to-Ankeny)Ultra-Low (Feels local)
DisplayMirror's physical monitorCan create a "Virtual" display
RequirementWorks on almost anythingBoth Macs must be Apple Silicon

4. Updating your Fish Function

To ensure your mini command always stays in its lane, you can actually chain the defaults write into your function. This ensures that even if you used High Performance for a different machine earlier, it resets to Standard for your Mini:

function mini
    # Force the app to use Standard mode
    defaults write com.apple.ScreenSharing "lastSelectedConnectionType" -int 1
    # Open the IPv6 connection
    open vnc://austinrognes@[fd7a:115c:a1e0::9a33:4161]
end

Why use Standard?

Standard is often better for your specific 2D game development workflow if you are:

  1. Headless: High Performance sometimes fails if there is no physical monitor or "Ghost Plug" in the Mini.
  2. Resource Heavy: High Performance uses the Mini's GPU to encode the video stream; Standard is lighter on the remote GPU, leaving more overhead for your game engine.

Is the High Performance mode giving you trouble with the screen resolution, or are you just looking for a more consistent connection over that IPv6 pipe?

turns.prompt_text: what if I force it to high-performance as they are both apple silicon devices?
turns.response_html:
If you've got Apple Silicon on both ends, High Performance is the way to go. It essentially turns your screen share into a low-latency video stream using the hardware encoders on your M-series chips. This is especially useful for your 2D game development, as it handles high-frame-rate movement much better than the standard VNC "blocky" updates.

Here is how to force that transition.

1. Update the Connection Type

To force the Screen Sharing app to prefer the High Performance protocol, you need to update the defaults for the app.

Run this on your MacBook Air:

defaults write com.apple.ScreenSharing "lastSelectedConnectionType" -int 2

2. The High-Performance URI

While vnc:// will often negotiate up to High Performance if both sides support it, you can sometimes explicitly trigger the modern handshake using the vm-connect scheme.

Try this command:

open vm-connect://austinrognes@[fd7a:115c:a1e0::9a33:4161]

3. Updated Fish Function

Since you’re all about that terminal efficiency, here is the updated function for your config.fish. This version ensures the app is set to High Performance every time you launch the connection to Ankeny.

function mini
    # Force High Performance (Type 2)
    defaults write com.apple.ScreenSharing "lastSelectedConnectionType" -int 2
    # Open the modern connection
    open vnc://austinrognes@[fd7a:115c:a1e0::9a33:4161]
end

(Note: I kept it as vnc:// in the function because macOS is often more stable at resolving the initial handshake through that scheme before upgrading the session to High Performance automatically.)

Why High Performance is Worth It

Since you’re bridging the gap between Ames and Ankeny, the difference in "feel" is significant:

  • Color Accuracy: It supports 4:4:4 chroma subsampling, which means text won't have that weird "fuzzy" fringe effect often seen in standard VNC.
  • Latency: It uses the H.264/H.265 hardware media engines. This reduces the "heavy" feeling of the mouse cursor.
  • Virtual Displays: In High Performance mode, you can actually create a virtual display with a resolution that matches your MacBook Air perfectly, rather than being stuck with whatever the Mac Mini's physical resolution is.

One Critical Catch: The "Headless" Problem

High Performance mode relies heavily on the Mac Mini's GPU. If that Mini is sitting in Ankeny without a monitor plugged into it, the GPU might not "start" a frame buffer, which can lead to a black screen or a failed connection.

If you get a connection error now that you've switched to High Performance, it's likely because the Mini is headless. You have two options:

  1. Revert to Standard: Use the -int 1 command from earlier.
  2. Hardware Cheat: Plug a cheap HDMI Dummy Plug (EDID emulator) into the Mini. This tricks the M-series chip into thinking a 4K monitor is attached, enabling full hardware acceleration for your remote session.

Do you notice a difference in the cursor response time now that you've flipped the switch to High Performance?

turns.prompt_text: open vm-connect://austinrognes@[fd7a:115c:a1e0::9a33:4161] No application knows how to open URL vm-connect://austinrognes@[fd7a:115c:a1e0::9a33:4161] (Error Domain=NSOSStatusErrorDomain Code=-10814 "kLSApplicationNotFoundErr: E.g. no application claims the file" UserInfo={_LSLine=1973, _LSFunction=runEvaluator, _LSFile=LSBindingEvaluator.mm, _LSErrorMessage=kLSApplicationNotFoundErr}).
turns.response_html:
My apologies—vm-connect:// is a bit of a ghost protocol. While it's used internally by macOS for certain virtualization and high-performance handshakes, it isn't a publicly registered URI scheme that the open command can reliably hand off to an application.

To get High Performance working, we have to use the standard vnc:// "front door" but force the Screen Sharing app to choose the High Performance "room" once it opens.

The Reliable High-Performance Workflow

The Screen Sharing app reads its preferences when it launches. If the app is already running in the background, it might ignore the defaults change you just made.

Here is the updated logic for your Fish function to ensure the switch actually "takes":

function mini
    # 1. Close the app if it's already open to ensure it reloads preferences
    pkill "Screen Sharing"
    
    # 2. Force the connection type to High Performance (Type 2)
    defaults write com.apple.ScreenSharing "lastSelectedConnectionType" -int 2
    
    # 3. Open the connection using the standard URI
    open "vnc://austinrognes@[fd7a:115c:a1e0::9a33:4161]"
end

Why this works better

By using vnc://, you are using a protocol the system definitely knows how to handle. Because you set the lastSelectedConnectionType to 2 immediately beforehand, the Screen Sharing app will wake up, look at its instructions, and say, "Okay, the user wants High Performance for this next connection."

How to tell it worked

Once the window opens, look at the very top of the screen share window (the toolbar):

  • Standard: Usually shows a simple screen icon.
  • High Performance: Will often have a "High Performance" label or a small "Video" icon in the toolbar, and you'll notice the color looks significantly more vibrant (due to the 4:4:4 chroma).

A Note on IPv6 Syntax

In your error message, it looks like the brackets were handled correctly, but just a reminder to keep those quotes around the URL in your Fish function: open "vnc://...". This prevents the shell from trying to interpret the brackets as a globbing pattern.

One Final Optimization

If you find that the connection still feels like "Standard" mode, it might be because the Mac Mini in Ankeny has Remote Management turned on instead of Screen Sharing. High Performance specifically requires the "Screen Sharing" toggle to be the primary one active in System Settings > General > Sharing.

Does the toolbar in the window now indicate you've successfully stepped up to High Performance?
